claim: In December 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain at Bell Labs achieved transistor action in a germanium point-contact device (historical, 1947).
evidence: "John Bardeen & Walter Brattain achieve transistor action in a germanium point-contact device in December 1947." (CHM Silicon Engine, 1947 entry)

claim: In April 1952, over 100 representatives from 40 companies that had paid a $25,000 patent-licensing fee attended Bell Labs' Transistor Technology Symposium, spreading transistor know-how to firms including GE, RCA, Texas Instruments and Sony (historical, 1952).
evidence: "In April 1952, over 100 representatives from 40 companies that had paid a $25,000 patent-licensing fee came for a nine-day Transistor Technology Symposium"; "There were participants from such electronics titans as GE and RCA, as well as from then-small firms like Texas Instruments and Sony." (CHM Silicon Engine, 1952 entry)

metric.name: Transistor patent licence fee (Bell Labs, 1952)
metric.population: Fee paid by each of the 40 companies attending the 1952 symposium
metric.methodology: Historical account by museum; not disclosed

claim: On September 12, 1958 Jack Kilby successfully tested the first integrated circuit at Texas Instruments (historical, 1958).
evidence: "Successful Test of the First Integrated Circuit. Jack Kilby successfully tests the first integrated circuit at Texas Instruments to prove that resistors and capacitors could exist on the same piece of semiconductor material." (CHM This Day in History, September 12)

claim: Jack Kilby received half of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics 'for his part in the invention of the integrated circuit'.
evidence: Prize motivation: "for his part in the invention of the integrated circuit" (Nobel Prize in Physics 2000 summary page)

claim: Jean Hoerni at Fairchild wrote a patent disclosure for the planar process in January 1959 and demonstrated a working planar transistor in March 1959; planar devices allowed all components of an integrated circuit to be fabricated from one side of a wafer (historical, 1959).
evidence: "After writing a patent disclosure in January 1959, he demonstrated a working planar transistor that March." ... "they permitted fabrication of all the components of an integrated circuit from one side of a wafer." (CHM Silicon Engine, 1959 planar entry)

claim: Robert Noyce (Fairchild) filed his monolithic integrated circuit patent in July 1959, and Fairchild engineers produced the first working monolithic ICs by May 1960 (historical).
evidence: paraphrase: CHM Silicon Engine 1959 entry states Noyce filed his patent in July 1959 and Fairchild engineers produced working monolithic ICs by May 1960; quote on concept: "By interconnecting diodes, transistors, resistors and capacitors diffused into the silicon with aluminum metal lines deposited on top of the protective oxide coating, one could configure complete electrical circuits on a single silicon chip."

claim: Gordon Moore's article 'Cramming more components onto integrated circuits' was published in Electronics on April 19, 1965, projecting a doubling of components per chip every 12 months; in 1975 he revised the rate to a doubling every two years (historical).
evidence: "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits" published in Electronics on April 19, 1965 ... "a doubling every 12 months"; in 1975 Moore slowed the forecast to "a doubling every two years, rather than every year." (CHM Silicon Engine, 1965 entry)

claim: Beginning in 1970, Intel's 1103 MOS DRAM, priced at 1 cent per bit, quickly replaced magnetic core memory for computer main memory (historical).
evidence: "Offering much faster speed and priced at 1 cent/bit, beginning in 1970 the 1103 quickly replaced magnetic core technology for computer main memory." (CHM Silicon Engine, 1970 entry)

claim: In 1971 Intel's 4004, a 4-bit CPU on a single chip with about 2,300 transistors, was implemented by Federico Faggin and Masatoshi Shima (historical; commonly described as the first commercial microprocessor).
evidence: "Ted Hoff and Stanley Mazor conceived Intel's first integrated CPU, the 4004 4-bit device ... In 1971, Federico Faggin, assisted by Masatoshi Shima, applied his experience in silicon-gate MOS technology ... to squeeze the 2300 transistors of the 4004 into a low-cost 16-pin package." (CHM Silicon Engine, 1971 entry)

claim: Between 1978 and 1986 the US share of the DRAM market fell from about 70% to 20% while the Japanese share rose from under 30% to about 75% (historical estimate).
evidence: "the U.S. market share plummeted from 70 to 20 percent between 1978 and 1986 as the Japanese share jumped from under 30 to about 75 percent." (Irwin 1996, NBER chapter, p. 7)
